summary:
Georgia stands under the United States national framework that governs every state. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passports are issued only as M or F from supporting documents, and passports already carrying an X remain valid until expiry. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs. A visitor whose documents no longer match their presentation should expect that mismatch to surface at federal checkpoints, where TSA secondary screening, devices and pat-downs carry an outing risk.

Entry screening follows national rules rather than Georgia law. The State Department announced in February 2025 a ban on trans athletes entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban for fraud. In April 2025 several foreign governments issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules; at least eight European governments, including Finland and Denmark, had already adjusted their guidance in March 2025.

Georgia has its own statute restricting care. Governor Brian Kemp signed Senate Bill 140 on 23 March 2023, barring licensed medical professionals from providing hormone therapy or gender-transition surgery to patients under 18, with licence revocation a possible penalty. The ban took effect on 1 July 2023. Minors who began hormone replacement therapy before that date may continue under the law, and the ACLU of Georgia announced at the time that it would sue. Nationally, gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and federal measures on youth care, including Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 and October 2025 proposals to bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18, have been blocked or enjoined in court in several cases.

Adult care in Georgia has contracted under federal funding pressure. On 13 February 2025 Memorial Health University Medical Center in Savannah abruptly cancelled all gender-affirming surgeries, including a pre-approved double mastectomy for a 24-year-old transgender man, citing a responsibility to follow state and federal laws and regulations. The Savannah Pride Center reported that at least two other area residents were also denied care. Visitors needing surgical or continuing gender-affirming care in Georgia should not assume a provider will proceed.

Violence against trans people in Georgia is documented and concentrated in Atlanta. In April 2023 the Atlanta Police Department said it was actively investigating three violent crimes against transgender women in the city that year, after two Black transgender women were fatally shot a week apart; a January 2023 shooting that left a transgender woman in critical condition also remained open. The department acknowledged the epidemic-level violence faced by Black and Brown transgender women. The state's recorded killing rate for trans women is 4.8 per 100,000 per year, a figure the monitoring project behind it describes as an acknowledged floor drawn from undercounted data.

Federal custody presents documented harm for anyone detained in Georgia. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men have reportedly been subjected to forced-labour programmes, with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups"; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.
tangentialFactors:
Facilities restrictions are a national pattern rather than a Georgia-specific finding. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states, while 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban; in some states trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

State document rules have tightened elsewhere in ways that set the direction of travel. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences and invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups describe it as a template for other states, with further targeting bills pending in state legislatures. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends. Georgia does not appear in that flag list.

The Georgia homicide figure sits alongside a documented national pattern of killings of Black transgender women, and the Atlanta Police Department's own 2023 statements placed the city's cases within that epidemic-level framing rather than treating them as isolated incidents.
localsOnly:
Georgia's State Health Benefit Plan is required to pay for medically necessary gender-affirming care for employees, spouses and dependants. Plaintiffs announced a settlement to that effect in an Atlanta federal court in October 2023, following a December 2022 lawsuit that argued the plan discriminated unlawfully by refusing to pay. Under the settlement the plan could be required to cover care for minors outside Georgia even though such care is prohibited inside the state, and coverage for public employees continued despite Senate Bill 140.

Senate Bill 140 binds licensed medical professionals in Georgia and exposes them to licence revocation. Its carve-out for minors already on hormone replacement therapy before 1 July 2023 means a resident who began treatment before that date may continue it under the statute.

The statewide count of killings of trans women, 4.8 per 100,000 per year, is produced by an undercounted monitoring project and functions as a floor, not a full measure of fatalities among residents.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any provision of Georgia's Senate Bill 140 has been enjoined or otherwise altered in the courts since it took effect on 1 July 2023 is unresolved in the available sources; the inventory records only that the ACLU of Georgia said it would sue.

Whether other Georgia hospitals cancelled or paused gender-affirming surgery or hormone care after February 2025 is not sourced. The Memorial Health cancellation in Savannah and the denials reported by the Savannah Pride Center are the only documented instances in this inventory.

Whether the terms of the 2023 State Health Benefit Plan settlement have been amended, litigated further or continued to be honoured after 2023 is not sourced here.

Georgia-specific legislation on identity documents, bathroom access or athlete participation in the 2025 and 2026 state legislative sessions is not sourced. The document-rule and facilities material in this dossier derives from other states and from national tallies.

The 4.8 per 100,000 killing rate is not attributed to a specific year range in the source, and the underlying monitoring project's methodology is not described beyond being acknowledged as undercounted.
